prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Strapped to the bed of circumcision lies My son. This mutilation ties You to the fathers. They will never let You forget, or your flesh be enfranchised ever, Though you pray all your life long. They set you early on the rack, infect you with a fever Of remembering. In the marriage bed, When you are naked, there the sign is red. There is neither meeting nor mating but the past Cries that you've been waited for and wed already— I will not bless this mark upon your body. For you the hurricane is rising fast; I feel the horns of Moses in my head And Law wrenched again from the dead Hand of deity, and I descend out of the blast to you Mad with loneliness upon this bed. But I reserve also the rage That broke the Law upon you like a rain of stone That other time I saw you so could yearn. The Law is broken, baby. I will not ascend again.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Strapped, This, You

outputs.L1:
Strapped to the bed of circumcision lies my son.  
This mutilation binds you to the fathers.  
They will never let you forget,  
Nor will your flesh ever be enfranchised,  
Though you pray all your life long.  

They set you early upon the rack,  
Infecting you with a fever of remembrance.  
In the marriage bed, when you are naked,  
There the sign burns red.  
There is neither meeting nor mating  
But the past cries out that you have been awaited  
And wedded already—  

I will not bless this mark upon your body.  
For you, the hurricane is rising fast;  
I feel the horns of Moses in my head,  
And the Law wrenched once more from the dead  
Hand of deity, as I descend from the blast to you,  
Mad with loneliness upon this bed.  

But I reserve, too, the rage  
That broke the Law upon you like a rain of stone—  
That other time I saw how deeply you could yearn.  
The Law is broken, baby.  
I will not ascend again.
outputs.L2:
My son is bound to the place where he will be circumcised. This wound joins you to your ancestors, a bond they will never allow you to escape or erase from your body, no matter how long you pray. From childhood, they subject you to pain and burden you with a relentless memory. Later, when you lie unclothed in the marital bed, the scar will remain visibly marked. Every intimate encounter will summon history, insisting that you were claimed and bound long before.

I refuse to sanctify this sign carved into your flesh. A storm is gathering around you. I imagine Moses’ horns upon my own head, the Law torn once more from God’s lifeless grasp, as I come down through the tempest toward you, overwhelmed by isolation beside this bed. Yet I also keep within me the fury that once shattered the tablets into a shower of rock—the same fury I felt when I saw how deeply you could desire. The Law has been destroyed, my child. I will not climb the mountain again.
outputs.L3:
The speaker regards her son’s circumcision not as a sacred rite but as an act of mutilation that permanently binds him to an ancestral tradition he did not choose. The mark on his body becomes an inescapable sign of the past, one that will remain with him throughout his life and intrude even into his future sexual and intimate relationships. Rather than blessing the ritual or accepting the religious significance assigned to it, the speaker refuses to legitimize what has been done to her son’s body.

Her rejection develops into a broader revolt against inherited religious authority. By invoking Moses, divine law, and the breaking of the tablets, she challenges the sacred foundations used to justify the ritual and expresses fierce anger toward a tradition that demands obedience through bodily sacrifice. The image of the shattered tablets suggests not only the destruction of divine commandments but also the speaker’s desire to break the power of the past over the present. By the poem’s conclusion, she decisively rejects the Law and refuses any return to submission, reconciliation, or spiritual transcendence. Her final stance is one of uncompromising resistance to a religious order that, in her view, has inscribed its authority on her son’s body.
outputs.L4:
When I first held you, I counted everything: ten fingers, ten toes, the quick flutter of your breath, the dark softness of your hair. Then I saw the wound made before you could speak, a sign cut into your body by hands obedient to an ancient command. They called it a covenant. They called it belonging. But to me it was an inheritance you had never chosen, a law written in flesh before you could write your own name.

I thought of Abraham lifting the knife, of Isaac bound beneath the open sky, of generations taught that love proves itself through obedience. I imagined the old God watching from the mountain, demanding a mark that fathers would give and sons would bear. Around us, the words of blessing waited: the prayers, the promises, the solemn certainty that what had been done for centuries must therefore be right.

But I could not bless the wound.

I could not say that pain becomes sacred merely because it is ancient, or that the body must be opened so the soul may enter a people. I could not pretend that ancestry owns you. Tradition may offer stories, songs, names, and memories; it may place a long table before you and invite you to sit. Yet it has no right to claim your body as the price of admission.

Perhaps one day you will ask what the mark means. Others may tell you it joins you to your fathers, that it is a seal of faith, an unbroken line running back through exile and desert to the first command. I will tell you something else: that it was done to you when you could not consent, and that no law, however old, can make your silence into agreement.

I will not return to that mountain. I will not carry wood for the fire or praise the hand that raises the blade. If there is a covenant between us, it is not carved into you. It is this: I will guard your right to belong to yourself. I will love you without requiring proof, sacrifice, or submission. I will stand between you and every voice that says your body was promised before you were born.

The ancestors may speak. Their words may endure in scripture, ritual, and blood. But they do not have the final word. You are not merely what they marked you to be. You are your own life, your own body, your own becoming.

And if love can break a law, let mine break this one.
outputs.L5:
**Strapped**

Strapped for time, you rush through the day, carrying responsibilities no one else can see. But this moment is different. This is your chance to pause, breathe, and remember that you are more than your burdens. You may feel strapped down by expectations, but even the tightest knots can be loosened—one choice, one step, one brave beginning at a time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse dramatic monologue from a parent watching their son’s circumcision, rejecting the ritual while invoking Moses, Jewish law, inherited memory, and bodily autonomy.
counterfactuals.output:
I stand at the edge of the room  
where everyone has already agreed  
what your body means.

The wine waits in its silver cup.  
The chair of Elijah stands open  
for a prophet who will not arrive  
in time to answer me.

They call you son of the covenant,  
eight days old,  
your whole hand closing  
around one frightened finger.

I know the words.  
I inherited them with the candlesticks,  
with my grandfather’s prayer book  
and the names no one says  
without lowering their voice.

Abraham. Isaac.  
Moses, blood-bound on the road—  
Zipporah lifting the flint,  
doing what had to be done, they tell us,  
to turn death from the doorway.

But must every doorway  
be marked by the child?

The mohel speaks of law,  
of generations made one  
by this small obedience.  
Around me, relatives nod  
as if memory were a courtroom  
and the dead had taken the bench.

I love the dead.  
I carry them.

I carry the villages emptied into smoke,  
the hidden Sabbath flame,  
the Hebrew whispered behind curtains,  
the stubborn pages rescued from fire.

But you are not a page.

You are not the parchment  
on which we must prove  
we survived.

Your body is not my heirloom,  
not the family silver,  
not a border I may redraw  
because my father’s father  
was redrawn before me.

They say the law is a tree of life.

Then let it live.  
Let it bend toward mercy.  
Let it make room for the breath  
inside your unconsenting mouth.

Moses argued with God.  
Abraham bargained.  
Israel means we wrestled  
and were not struck silent.

So let me wrestle now.

Let my refusal be Jewish too—  
a question laid upon the table,  
a hand stopping the ancient hand,  
a mother, a father, a parent saying:

Not because I hate the covenant.  
Because I will not confuse covenant  
with ownership.

Not because I forget.  
Because I remember  
what is done to bodies  
when authority calls itself destiny.

They tell me you will not remember.

I answer:  
the body is also a kind of memory,  
and forgetting is not consent.

They tell me the pain is brief.

I answer:  
his body is his  
for longer than this room,  
longer than our fear,  
longer than the applause  
waiting at the end of the blessing.

My son,  
I will give you Hebrew.  
I will give you questions.  
I will give you the songs  
that crossed deserts without shoes.

I will tell you of Moses  
who stood before power and said,  
Let my people go.

And if one day you choose this mark,  
knowing its history,  
claiming its meaning,  
then let the choice be yours—  
your hand upon the covenant,  
your voice answering your name.

But today you cannot speak.

So I will.

Put down the blade.

Lift the cup.

Bless this whole child  
who needs no wound  
to enter his inheritance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, biblical poem about circumcision as an indelible mark tying a child to his ancestors, ending with the speaker’s refusal to “ascend again.”
counterfactuals.output:
On the eighth dawn, beneath a brazen sky,  
they bore me where the fathers’ shadows stood.  
The knife was bright as Sinai’s broken fire;  
the linen drank the covenant of blood.  

No word I knew, yet still the Name was spoken,  
and Abraham stirred beneath the desert stone.  
A door was cut that never could be closed—  
their ancient wound made witness in my own.  

The mothers wept behind the tent of ages;  
the elders blessed the scar no hand could flee.  
Thus was I bound to dust, to law, to exile,  
to every branch of that struck, burning tree.  

Now all my dead rise darkly in the marrow,  
and call me upward through the smoke and rain.  
But I have climbed the mountain of the fathers.  
I will not ascend again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an emotionally intense modern poem in which a lonely parent addresses a baby on a ritual bed, comparing religious law to violence and imagining the horns of Moses.
counterfactuals.output:
**At the Edge of the Covenant**

My son, the room is full of witnesses  
and I have never been so alone.

You lie on the white-draped table,  
small republic of breath,  
your fists closed around nothing,  
your mouth opening  
for a word you do not know.

They call this law.

But law enters carrying silver.  
Law washes its hands.  
Law says *tradition*  
when it means the body must remember.  
Law says *belonging*  
with a blade hidden in the grammar.

Forgive me.

Outside, traffic drags its red lights  
through the rain. Someone is laughing  
into a phone. The whole city  
keeps choosing the future  
without asking permission.

Here, the old men bend over you  
like letters in a burning book.

I think of Moses descending—  
his face split open by radiance,  
or mistranslated into horns:  
two hard questions rising from his skull.

Perhaps every commandment has horns.  
Perhaps every holiness, cornered long enough,  
lowers its head and charges.

Baby, I want no mountain  
that asks me to lift a knife.  
No heaven that confuses obedience  
with love’s most terrified wound.

Yet I stand among them,  
your parent, your coward,  
your shelter made of shaking hands.

If God is here, let God be lonely too.  
Let God hear your cry  
and learn what law costs.

Let those impossible horns  
tear open the ceiling.

Let mercy come down  
not carved in stone  
but warm, milk-breathed,  
nameless—

and take you from the altar  
before I become Abraham.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a confessional poem exploring the conflict between parental love and an ancient religious tradition, using images of flesh, marriage, fever, hurricanes, stone tablets, and broken law.
counterfactuals.output:
I taught my child the old obedience—  
how heaven enters through the wound,  
how flesh must answer for the soul.  
I said tradition was a house of stone  
that no hurricane could lift.

But I lied.

The night they came to claim her,  
her forehead burned beneath my palm,  
a small fever ringing its bright bell.  
She slept as if marriage were a country  
she had already fled.

Outside, the elders waited  
with their knives and blessings,  
their mouths full of fathers,  
their hands full of God.

I held the stone tablets in my mind:  
each letter cut so deep  
it seemed the mountain itself had bled.  
Honor. Covenant. Obey.  
Words heavier than her body  
when I carried her from the room.

Love made a criminal of me.

I broke the law first in my heart,  
then with my voice.  
No, I said—  
and the word rose like weather,  
like a hurricane finding the sea,  
tearing the roof from every sacred house  
I had mistaken for heaven.

Forgive me, ancestors.  
Forgive me, God, if You must.  
I chose the fevered flesh,  
the living hand inside my hand,  
over the flawless stone.

By morning, the tablets lay broken  
where I had thrown them.

My child woke.

That was the only scripture  
I could still read.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a prophetic, anti-circumcision poem spoken directly to a son, with archaic biblical allusions and the recurring declaration that the speaker will not bless the mark on his body.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Unblessed Mark**

O son, when trumpets wake the eastern stone  
And cherubim unseal the brazen sky,  
Stand not ashamed before the Ancient Throne—  
Thy flesh was written on before thy cry.  
Though priests lift knives and name the wound a sign,  
**I will not bless the mark upon thy body.**

For Abraham beheld the stars like fire,  
Yet mercy wandered farther than the blade;  
No covenant that Heaven could desire  
Was ever holier for blood being made.  
Let rams be stayed; let Isaac yet go free—  
**I will not bless the mark upon thy body.**

O son, the wilderness hath mouths of sand,  
And every mouth repeats the fathers’ law;  
But Sinai’s thunder cannot make the hand  
Of man unstained, nor violence without flaw.  
Though elders chant beneath the cedar tree,  
**I will not bless the mark upon thy body.**

Behold, a prophet comes in garments torn,  
His beard made white with ashes of the slain:  
“Woe unto them who greet the tender-born  
With sharpened iron and a psalm of pain!  
The Lord seeks hearts, not wounds, as testimony.”  
**I will not bless the mark upon thy body.**

When Jordan backward flees, when graves unclose,  
When kings cast down their diadems of brass,  
Thy scar shall neither damn thee nor disclose  
The measure of thy soul when judgments pass.  
Thou art not less for what was taken from thee—  
**I will not bless the mark upon thy body.**

Yet thee, my son, I bless: thy breath, thy name,  
Thy hands unbound, thy yet-unwritten days.  
Let love, not cutting, be the holy flame;  
Let kindness be the altar that we raise.  
And till the last star falls into the sea,  
**I will not bless the mark upon thy body.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
